Expelled
ex-peld'
v. (driven out by force; of the Canaanites Israel did not expel, of Anak's sons Caleb did, and of the apostles driven from Antioch's coasts)
From Latin expellere, to drive out, from ex and pellere, to drive. The Hebrew at Joshua 13:13 is yarash, to dispossess or take possession by driving out; the Greek at Acts 13:50 is ekballo, to cast out.

Biblical Definition

The word runs along the fault line of the conquest narratives. On the failure side: “Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day” (Joshua 13:13). The book of Judges opens with a whole catalogue of such failures, and the consequences run through the rest of the Old Testament — the nations left in the land became the snare God said they would be. On the obedience side stands one old man: “And they gave Hebron unto Caleb, as Moses said: and he expelled thence the three sons of Anak” (Judges 1:20). Caleb was eighty-five and asked for the hill country with the giants on it, because the LORD had promised it forty-five years earlier and he had not stopped believing it. In the New Testament the direction reverses and the church is on the receiving end: “the Jews stirred up the devout and honourable women, and the chief men of the city, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts” (Acts 13:50). Luke adds immediately that the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines expel as to drive or force out, to eject, and also to banish or exclude from a society.

expand to see more

EXPELLED, pp. Driven out or away; forced to leave; banished; exiled; ejected.

EXPEL, v.t. To drive or force out from any inclosed place; as, to expel wind from the stomach.

2. To drive out; to force to leave; to eject; as, to expel an enemy from a country.

3. To banish; to exile; to force to quit a country.

4. To exclude; to keep out or off; as, to expel a member of a society.

Key Scripture

Joshua 13:13 — "Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day."

Judges 1:20 — "And they gave Hebron unto Caleb, as Moses said: and he expelled thence the three sons of Anak."

Acts 13:50 — "But the Jews stirred up the devout and honourable women, and the chief men of the city, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts."

Acts 13:52 — "And the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost."

Modern Corruption

The conquest is judged by modern political categories, and the far more relevant lesson — what Israel's incomplete obedience cost — is left unpreached.

expand to see more

Contemporary discussion of Joshua fixes almost entirely on the morality of the conquest, and the church has often been more anxious about that question than the text is. Scripture's own framing is judicial: the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full in Abraham's day and was full four hundred years later; the land is said to spew out its inhabitants for their abominations, and Israel is warned in the same breath that it will spew her out too if she does the same. The conquest is presented as an act of divine judgment executed by a commissioned instrument, not as a national land grab with a religious excuse, and the identical judgment fell on Israel when she earned it.

The lesson the church most needs from these texts is the one about incompleteness. They expelled not — and the peoples left in the land became exactly the snare the LORD had said they would be, drawing Israel into the idolatry that ended in exile. Every generation of believers has its Geshurites: sins not driven out but tolerated at the border, on the reasoning that they are small, or useful, or too costly to remove. Caleb is the counter-example and he is instructive precisely because his portion was the hardest — the hill country, with the giants — and he took it at eighty-five on the strength of a promise made when he was forty.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yarash, to dispossess — Joshua 13:13; garash, to drive out — Judges 1:20; Greek ekballo, to cast out — Acts 13:50; Latin expellere, to drive out.

expand to see more

Hebrew yarash — to take possession by dispossessing; Joshua 13:13, the word of the conquest.

Hebrew garash — to drive out, expel; Judges 1:20 of Caleb and the sons of Anak.

Hebrew Anaqim — the Anakim, the giants whose report frightened ten of the twelve spies.

Greek ekballo — to cast out; Acts 13:50, of Paul and Barnabas driven from the coasts.

Latin expellere, from pellere, to drive — the source of the English word.

Usage

"“The children of Israel expelled not” — and the nations left became the snare foretold."

"“He expelled thence the three sons of Anak” — Caleb at eighty-five, on a promise forty-five years old."

"“Expelled them out of their coasts” — and the disciples were filled with joy."
